title: Harar, the walled city
hookLine: the walled city of Ethiopia, crowded with mosques and saints' shrines

lines: AN OLD WALL ON A HILL.
LANES FULL OF MOSQUES AND TOMBS.
cards: After dark, outside the old wall of a hilltop city in eastern Ethiopia, a man sits on the ground with a basket of scraps and calls out names. Out of the night come hyenas.
He feeds them, sometimes from a stick held in his teeth. In this city, people say, the hyenas and the townsfolk have an old agreement: the animals are fed, and they leave the people alone.
Inside the wall, the lanes twist, the houses are painted in bright colors, and every few turns there's another small mosque or the tomb of a holy man. Today: Harar.

teach.h: A STORY REACHING BACK TO THE REFUGE.
teach.b: Ethiopia has a long Christian history, and also a Muslim story reaching back to the first refuge, when early Muslims found safety with the king of Abyssinia.
Sahih al-Bukhari even records that when that king died, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions and led a funeral prayer for him.

teach.h: A WALLED CITY IN THE HIGHLANDS.
teach.b: Harar grew up later, in the highlands of the east, as a Muslim trading town and a center of learning. Its old city is closed in by a wall with gates, and inside, the town is thick with mosques, shrines and tombs.
Tradition calls Harar the city of saints.
The saints here are the awliya, the friends of God: scholars and holy people whose graves are cared for, visited and prayed beside.
Tradition also names a founding saint, Sheikh Abadir, said to have come from Arabia and settled the town.

Muslims differ about visiting saints' tombs. Sufi tradition treasures it as a way of honoring the friends of God; other Muslims hold that prayer belongs at the mosque and that visits to graves should be kept simple.
Harar holds a strong Sufi tradition, and its shrines are part of the city's life. Hararis have their own language too, Harari, once written in Arabic letters.
A walled city with its own tongue and its own saints, in a land where churches and mosques have stood side by side for a very long time.

how: In Harar, people visit the shrines of the city's saints, and Muslims pray in its many small mosques inside the old wall.

games.q: you're a visitor in Harar's old city at dusk. you hear that someone is feeding hyenas just outside the wall. what do you do?
o: go and watch, standing back with the townspeople.
ask to leave the city before dark.
games.why: visitors and townspeople gather to watch the hyena feeding, an old custom of the city, and the hyenas take their scraps and go.

practice: Here is one Ethiopian word: selam, which in Amharic, Ethiopia's widely spoken language, means peace and is used as a greeting, close to the Arabic salam.
Say it softly, let it sit on the breath in and the breath out, and bring to mind one person you'd like to greet with peace, maybe someone it's hard to greet.
If you pray, ask peace for them; if not, simply hold the word and the person together.

wordCard.voice: Harar. The walled Muslim city of eastern Ethiopia, crowded with mosques and the tombs of its saints. Today's word.
